correctness.rationale: The claim is proved exactly for all \(\mu>0\), \(0<\alpha<1/2\), and \(\tau>0\). Gaussian covariance gives independence; the exact discovery probability follows by standardization. Strict concavity follows from \(g(x)=\log\Phi(x)\) having \(g''(x)=-h(x)(x+h(x))<0\), together with negative second derivatives of the sine/cosine inner means. Endpoint derivative signs give a unique root, the derivative at \(\pi/4\) gives \(\tau_*>1\), and the root equation gives the weak-signal limit. The bundled verifier recomputes reported values; finite computations are treated only as checks, not as the proof.

originality.rationale: No inspected source or database record states the same scalar joint-selection-and-confirmation optimization, its unique inverse-Mills root, the strict \(\tau_*>1\) conclusion for all positive signals, and the weak-signal closed form. The closest modern paper exposes the tunable information split but stops short of this objective-specific allocation law. Cox (1975) is retained as a material residual risk because its abstract discusses optimal proportions for a different many-normal-means data-splitting problem and its full formulas were unavailable.
residual_risks: Cox (1975) could contain an equivalent split-fraction calculation under its many-normal-means formulation; only the abstract was accessible, so its exact implication was not resolved.
An older normal-theory screening/confirmation paper may express the same root under ordinary data-splitting rather than fission terminology.
The novelty claim is therefore limited to the inspected literature and database searches; it is not a proof of global bibliographic uniqueness.

value.rationale: The fission noise level directly allocates Fisher information between model screening and confirmation, and modern source literature explicitly leaves variance selection as a design question. For the canonical scalar benchmark, the exact optimizer is structurally nontrivial: every conventional one-sided level forces more information to confirmation than screening, and the weak-signal allocation has a closed form. At \(\alpha=0.05\), the local selection share is only \(0.1301507268\), providing a concrete benchmark that differs sharply from equal splitting. The null-boundary joint rejection probability remains exactly \(\alpha/2\) for all allocations, clarifying the source of the gain.
